Latent Anomaly Knowledge Excavation: Unveiling Sparse Sensitive Neurons in Vision-Language Models

Excavate anomaly-sensitive neurons already present in a vision-language model using a small set of normal samples.

Li Shaotian · Li Shangze · Shi Chuancheng · Wu Wenhua · Wu Yanqiu · Yu Xiaohan · Shen Fei · Chua Tat-Seng

April 9, 2026 ·ACM Multimedia 2026 ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

LAKE treats anomaly detection as eliciting latent pretrained knowledge. A sparse set of sensitive neurons supports a compact normality representation without gradient-based training.

SparseSensitive-neuron representation
NormalSamples used for localization
0Gradient-based backbone updates

Why this matters

Treating a VLM as a black-box feature extractor can obscure which internal signals support anomaly detection. LAKE examines whether those signals can be selected and elicited directly.

How it works

  1. Use a minimal set of normal samples to identify anomaly-sensitive neurons in the pretrained model.
  2. Isolate the selected signals to construct a compact representation of normality.
  3. Combine visual structural deviations with cross-modal semantic activations for anomaly scoring.

What the study finds

Evaluation on industrial anomaly-detection benchmarks reports strong performance together with neuron-level interpretability. The approach uses normal samples and does not train a new backbone.

What this means

Anomaly-specific adaptation is not the only route to a detector: carefully selected pretrained signals can provide another basis for downstream inspection.
